content.introduction: This week's economic calendar, as reported by Kiplinger, includes a light but steady stream of data starting with results of two services purchasing managers' surveys on Monday. Key highlights include the release of the minutes from the September Fed meeting and preliminary October sentiment survey results on Friday. The labor market data and consumer spending remain stable and strong, although there is a noted widening gap between consumer sentiment and spending behavior, influenced by high gasoline prices, mortgage rates, and inflation expectations. The sources do not provide a definitive answer to specific questions about the exact figures or detailed outcomes of these reports.
body:
At the same time, labor market data and consumer spending remain stable, strong, even, for the latter.

With specific regard to the Conference Board survey, William Blair economist Richard de Chazal observes a widening gap "between how consumers feel and how they spend."

But he also notes a difficult survey period for households, including gasoline near $4.50 a gallon, 30-year mortgage rates above 7%, a 10-year Treasury yield at its highest level since 2007 and a Fed set to raise rates again. [...] "Prices were the dominant concern," the economist concludes. Indeed, consumers' inflation expectations weighed on the Michigan index. That's the trend Fed Chair Kevin Warsh and his fellow voting members of the FOMC will watch.

As Chazal concludes, "A weakening consumer argues for patience, while rising inflation expectations leave room for further policy restriction."

### Friday (10/9)

Noteworthy economic reports [...] This week's economic calendar includes the minutes from the September Fed meeting and preliminary October sentiment survey results.
